My thoughts, (this issue is not limited to Copilot)
First a couple of serious concerns:

* With regards to AI generated or partially generated code: I think the project should not accept it (beyond trivial changes), and be explicit about it in the contribution guidelines. Why: a) Contributors must have rights over the code they contribute and sign it off. With code produced by an AI agent a contributor cannot know where it came from. With some agents collating search results and LLM generated filler, we are likely to end up in a situation where the AI agent is just hidding the fact the code is somebody elses copyrighted/not compatibly licensed code. b) AI generated code can look ok in a first look but be completely incorrect or pointless, while a too permisive or quick reviewer may accept it. Being AI generated means the barrier for a contributor to generate and submit it is very low (and therefore the code may also not be even tested or built at all, we have seen this already in PRs). The risk for crud getting in, and reviewers time waste is too high.

* About commit messages, PR desciptions or answers to discussions: We should be explicit about requiring contributors to either write them themselves or be very critical about any AI generated ones. Why: We have already several examples of PRs descriptions, commits and PR messages generated by AI, where the user did not disclose this fact, and where on a quick isolated first look the PR description or commit message seems ok, but then it becomes evident they do not match the actual commits. LLMs are very good at generating "correctly sounding" text, which does not need to be factually correct. At best this will waste reviewers time and create pointless confusion. At worst: a) crud will get in our repository, and b) we end up in a situation where we have "contributors" acting as interfaces to AI agents, copy pasting the discussion and copying the AI agent responses, wasting reviewers time in senseless back and forths, or even worse, somebody automates an AI agent to do it automatically without the human middleman. (As maintainer I absolutely do not want to waste my time, thinking I'm helping a new contributor, being patient trying to explain things, while all I'm doing is wasting my time interacting with a prentender AI agent).

I think both of these are real serious issues we are starting to face. And that unless we are clear about from today, will just get much worse over time.

About usign Copilot in reviews:
* I would be quite wary of it and specially about starting to use it systematically or using any money on it. To me it seems like MS is just offering the technology for free/for cheap by now while they mature it so they are covering the cost while they beta test it with us. The technology may improve, but if it does, the cost will certainly raise. This technology is quite a resource burner, so if the cost is passed to us, I cannot imagine it would be worthwhile our projects money any time soon if anybody can just press the "copilot do some work now" button. GitHubs CI is hardly price competitive, I cannot imagine Copilot would be.

So far I have seen copilot provide some valid review feedback (typos, or some issues a static analyzer could also detect) and some other pointless/senseless. I can also imagine Copilot would help somebody understand a PR in some cases they otherwise wouldn't, but you may also wonder that if a reviewer needs copilot to explain them a PR, maybe they should not be reviewing that PR, or even worst, base their feedback on the understanding they just gained from a Copilot generated explanation.

about AI assisted reviews, they actually fall under AI generated code, i.e. if the Copilot bot suggests a code change and the suggestion is appled, it is a AI generated code and we need some guidelines around this.

I think the topic of code provenance (copyrighted code / license incompatibility) is actually orthogonal. As pointed out by @P01 recently, the project needs some code scanning tools to help us look for matches in existing code bases, and flag any potential issue in contributions (and in code that's already in-tree... 🫣).

We've seen many contributions where people just "naively" copy-paste Linux code, or just change SPDX license in copyright headers of files they "borrowed" somewhere else, long before AI was the new cool kid on the block.

Similarly, we don't really require folks making suggestions in reviews to "sign off" on the snippets of code they are effectively "contributing", so I would again argue there is a lot of stuff that probably needs to be "tidied up" if tracking provenance really is a major concern (and it probably is, don't get me wrong!)

I agree with @P04's point that provenance is orthogonal. I also think we should acknowledge that regardless of policy folks will submit PRs with AI generated code in them, whether or not they acknowledge it. We're going to need some way to manage the risk no matter what we decide here.

I'd propose that even if we do use AI for review, we *do not* use it automatically. That any usage of AI for review should report an estimated carbon and monetary cost and a question about whether the submitter felt the review was worth the cost every time its used. The goal would be to dissuade unreasonable usages and waste, which are oh so easy to ignore without this sort of information directly presented back.

This is exactly what I mean by wasteful

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/90182#discussion_r2100472161

Notably we're talking about running an AI tool, a highly wasteful tool, to catch what an existing static analyzer would have found had we simply ran them.

I am not against AI in general so much, but there is one observation I do have to share which I don't know if it has been discussed yet.

One thing I have noticed from having people (and myself) running AI reviewers on my PRs, is that it is creating a lot of unnecessary work for me to go and try to understand a suggestion which is sometimes subtly incomprehensible at worst and flat out didn't make sense at best (yes, subtle is worse). And since sometimes the AI has valid points, it feels like there is an obligation to check all of them which may not be so easy to judge and require deciphering of what it means or squinting at the code to try to prove that there is something there or not. It's like a guilty until proven innocent situation. And I suppose this is the case with human reviewers to, but it seems a lot more rare for human reviewers to mess up so badly yet convincingly. Maybe it's common to have disagreements with human reviewers but that is actually productive because there really is an understanding for one or both people to be had there, whereas this AI does not benefit from being wrong, and it does not feel like as good of a use of time to validate or dispel it's suggestions as it is when coming from a human because it is often hallucinating and nobody is actually benefiting from that time sink.

Also, I am pretty sure I read something lately about a similar situation happening on like bug bounty websites. Apparently maintainers of open source projects are even now banning people who are submitting AI generated bug bounties because they are such detailed and convincing bug reports that people are submitting to try to claim some easy money, but they turn out to be completely hallucinated and wasting a monumental amount of maintainer time. This is obviously the fault of the people who submit the reports without even confirming what the AI said but it seems this general issue of wasting time due to something an AI generated is becoming an industry wide problem.

In terms of C static analysis tools you may very well be right, but I'm going to cheat just a little and point at rustc because it too is a static analyzer and actually... maybe not so shockingly... solves all of these issues without needing to pay anyone extra or burn forests down to train a bot. That said its infeasible to make Zephyr with Rust today or maybe ever due to various factors, but its still worth noting here.

I also found this great site from Carnegie Melon that breaks down a ton of common mistakes and which static analyzers find them for C/C++ and well worth a look https://wiki.sei.cmu.edu/

I've linked what I feel are likely relevant rules which have a table of static analyzers that would find them.

### [drivers: syscon: bflb efuses #89108 (review)](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/89108#pullrequestreview-2838075174)

Some tools appear to support flagging this sort of thing for C/C++ https://wiki.sei.cmu.edu/confluence/display/c/EXP46-C.+Do+not+use+a+bitwise+operator+with+a+Boolean-like+operand

rust and rustc fail to compile this sort of thing noting its not a boolean expression [rust playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=3d8dcfb861f288cf3f8d59cc1dbac697)

ultimately this is because C allows for implicitly interpreting integers as booleans, and we will forever be cursed with this in C or C++

### [samples: boards: espressif: ulp: Add interrupt sample #89662 (comment)](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/89662#discussion_r2081499197)

Looking at the code its mutated then printed in the interrupt directly after the mutation, volatile does nothing here really and the suggestion should have been to use atomics for the problem that the AI suggests is there in my opinion. Carnagie Melon seems to agree with me here and notes the tools that check for this.. https://wiki.sei.cmu.edu/confluence/display/c/CON43-C.+Do+not+allow+data+races+in+multithreaded+code

Rust and rustc would have failed to compile this and complained about a mutable global without synchronization or unsafe which atomics provide [rust playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=59e24ad9c4759902c60129df3e8d3250)

### [drivers: display: Re-introduce SSD1327 #87001 (review)](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/87001#pullrequestreview-2823494033)

This is maybe the only one where I'll say a C static analyzer may not have caught it but surely a static variable in a function is going to be a code smell in Zephyr land, though perhaps some of the same rules would apply https://wiki.sei.cmu.edu/confluence/display/c/CON43-C.+Do+not+allow+data+races+in+multithreaded+code

rust and rustc would have caught this as static/global mutables are unsafe without synchronization for exactly the same reason as the above global being mutated would fail to compile.

### Summary

Static tools can solve many more problems than we look for today,  https://wiki.sei.cmu.edu/ suggests a great set of rules and tools that work right now. Notably coverity does in fact cover many of these problems already.

Rust does almost all of this without any additional tooling or cost, and can be run anywhere by anyone at any time which is likely a huge boon to avoiding centralizing these things. But would require esoteric architecture support from the various hardware vendors which is likely untenable near or long term, maybe ever. At least directly.

Static analysis is absolutely possible to cover these and likely many many more bugs in a more consistent, repeated, and easily understandable manner than AI bots.

AI tools can, seemingly, be confidently incorrect and fool us all, just like the rest of us. They can also seemingly produce confusing made up comments that lead us astray and waste time.

Yes, but as I said "does not justify the problems that LLM may cause.".
Humans are teachable, especially from their mistakes. LLMs are not (and I do not want to train them). Also, people will likely question human/SCA reviews but blindly follow LLM. I remember a discussion in a review where someone just pulled arguments from an AI platform instead of looking at the C standard. These arguments were obviously completely wrong, yet no one questioned them. No one needs "unlimited" knowledge to contribute, we are not building on a fusion reactor (That would be the right project to spend money on instead of AI). Also, the SCA tool report may cause more harm than good (MISRA does not make it better). However, there is usually an analysis trace that a reviewer or author can follow and understand. The copilot output is just "Prisencolinensinainciusol".

Picking from @P07 and @P08 comments, I think that dumping AI generated comments on someone's PR is a bad approach (automatically or manually and not following up on it), imagine a new contributor getting a bunch of generated comment and nothing else, should they do it? Is the PR going be AI approved.

If an author wants to use AI tools for authoring code, or if a review wants to use AI tools as a reviewer tool so be it, it's not like the project has any control on that anyway. But then I'd expect the author/reviewer to stay ahead of their tools, in the same way as one is expected to stay ahead of their editor config, git workflow etc.

To me it all comes down to: if I can tell that your code or review comments are generated without you telling me, we are doing things wrong.

The ethic conversation is a bit of a more complex story but I think there's a difference between the project saying "you can use AI tools but be aware of it" and "we'll just fire up the thing on all PRs".

A pedantic question: At what point is this required (or expected given that it is just a "should")? Surely we do not need to provide information if we use Copilot for reviews, or if part of a function were co-developed with an LLM? 

Additionally, there are non-agent AI tools: This mentions AI-tools in general, but the format defined below

```
Assisted-by: [Agent Name]:[Model Version] [Tool1] [Tool2]
```

Seems to be agent specific. 

The wording `When AI tools are being used` is, IMO, significantly different from the wording `When AI tools contribute to kernel development` from https://kernel.org/doc/html//next/process/coding-assistants.html, as the latter imply agents and the former covers any AI tool.

From my point of view, reviews are not relevant in this regard. Neither using LLMs for minor autocomplete. On the other hand, from my point of view, once you start prompting to do changes or add new functions that would qualify.

> From my point of view, reviews are not relevant in this regard. Neither using LLMs for minor autocomplete. On the other hand, from my point of view, once you start prompting to do changes or add new functions that would qualify.

In some cases, I think you somewhat contradict yourself here. 

If a review from e.g. Copilot contains a code suggestion, and the submitter applies that code suggestion, then you technically use a change from a prompt :) In that case, should you add Copilot as an agent (using an unknown model?) in the commit where you applied a code suggestion from Copilot? 

I'm concerned about some of the language here, as it almost raises more questions for me than it answers. Specifically since it somewhat putting AI tool, LLM and AI Agent into the same box, when they are significantly different things (and in many cases are poorly defined)

Mostly I want to be sure whether the
```
Assisted-by: [Agent Name]:[Model Version] [Tool1] [Tool2]
```

part of commit only needs to be applied when AI agents are used, and what we consider an AI agent, and if we want to apply it to all AI tools and uses of e.g. LLMs, then the `[Agent Name]` part of it must be optional?
Perhaps it should made clearer that this applies to the use of GenAI for the code submitted in general, not just when used via the somewhat blurry term "an AI agent".

Isn't `GenAI` an equally blurry term? :D 

For example if I run a local LLM on my PC and that generates some code for me, then that's (probably?) GenAI, but is indeed not an agent, but the Copilot review agent is still GenAI I suspect? 

If I use e.g. 5 different local models for a commit, should all 5 be listed, or none of them since I'm not using an agent? 

Additionally if I use some GenAI tool, or agent, or whatever to write my Pull Request description (something may soon be very easy to do from the Github web UI: https://github.blog/changelog/2026-02-25-generate-pull-request-titles-with-copilot-on-the-web/), should the commits also be updated to reflect that?
